---
title: "Generating synthetic respondents in R"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

**Experimental.** This tutorial makes synthetic respondents from your own
instrument, personas and models, in R code. The
[app](app-tour.html) does the same steps on screen, with or without real
data. Synthetic respondents are for comparing models with the benchmark, or
for pretesting a scale before real data exist, not for replacing a field
test.

Everything below runs with the **mock** provider, which gives random answers
without calling an API. Swap in `sc_model("anthropic")`, `sc_model("openai")`
or `sc_model("ollama", ...)` for a real run.

```{r}
library(synthcheck)
```

## 1. The instrument

`sc_instrument()` takes an item table (`item`, `statement`, and optionally
`scale`, `facet` and `reverse`) or a plain vector of statements, plus the
response scale:

```{r}
ins <- sc_instrument(hexaco_items[hexaco_items$trait == "H", ], scale = c(1, 7),
                     name = "HEXACO Honesty-Humility")
ins
```

Labels default to agree-disagree labels for 5- and 7-point scales. Give your
own with `labels`, and your own text with `instructions`.

A template item table ships with the package:

```{r}
tpl <- system.file("templates", "instrument_template.csv", package = "synthcheck")
read.csv(tpl)
```

## 2. The personas

A persona is the system prompt: Who the synthetic respondent is. Type them,
or build every combination of a few attributes with `sc_persona_grid()`:

```{r}
per <- sc_persona_grid(age = c(25, 45, 65), gender = c("woman", "man"),
                       country = c("Canada", "the United States"),
                       template = "You are a {age}-year-old {gender} living in {country}.")
per
```

The attribute columns are kept in the generated data, so you can compare
groups later. `sc_personas()` takes a vector of descriptions or a table with
a `description` column (see
`system.file("templates", "personas_template.csv", package = "synthcheck")`).

## 3. The prompt

`sc_prompt()` shows exactly what is sent for one respondent:

```{r}
p <- sc_prompt(ins, per$description[1], items = ins$items$item[1:3])
cat(p$system, "\n\n", p$user, sep = "")
```

The model answers in structured JSON, one whole number per item. Answers
outside the scale and missing items are retried, then stored as `NA`.

## 4. The models

```{r}
sc_default_models
sc_model("anthropic", temperature = 1)
sc_model("ollama", "gemma3:27b", name = "Gemma 3 27B")
```

The defaults are the cheapest models of each provider that take a
temperature. `temperature = NULL` sends none, for models that do not take
one. API keys come from `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY` (for example
in `.Renviron`) and are never written to the saved files.

## 5. Generate

An **attempt** is one full pass over the personas, with `respondents`
respondents per persona. The number of calls is models × attempts × personas
× respondents.

```{r}
models <- list(sc_model("mock", name = "Mock A"), sc_model("mock", name = "Mock B"))
syn <- generate_synthetic(ins, models, per, attempts = 3, respondents = 10,
                          progress = FALSE, seed = 1)
dim(syn)
syn[1:3, 1:12]
```

Useful settings for real runs:

- `parallel`: How many calls run at the same time.
- `batch_size`: Respondents per call. The default, 1, keeps every respondent
  independent. Larger batches are cheaper, but respondents in one call may
  depend on each other.
- `block_size`: Items per call, for long instruments.
- `shuffle`: A new item order for every respondent.
- `output`: A folder. Each attempt is written there as soon as it is done,
  with the settings (`run.json`) and every prompt (`prompts.json`) beside it,
  so a stopped run keeps its finished attempts.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
syn <- generate_synthetic(ins, list(sc_model("anthropic"), sc_model("openai")), per,
                          attempts = 5, respondents = 10, parallel = 8,
                          output = "hexaco_run")
```

## 6. Save and read

```{r}
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write_synthetic(syn, f)
syn2 <- read_synthetic(f)
nrow(syn2)
```

`read_synthetic()` also reads a whole output folder back into one table.

## 7. Benchmark

`as_synthetic_list()` turns the long table into the list of models and
attempts that the benchmark takes:

```{r}
real <- hexaco_real[hexaco_real$country == "Canada", ]
bm <- authenticity_benchmark(as_synthetic_list(syn, items = ins$items$item), real, ins$items,
                             fit_scales = character(0), n_splits = 5, n_floor = 5)
bm
summarise_benchmark(bm)
```

Random answers score close to 0 on every column, as they should: 0 is what
shuffled real answers score. Real language models are not guaranteed to do
better. On HEXACO, the six models in `hexaco_llm` often fall below 0 because
their respondents bunch together; see [the benchmark](benchmark.html).
